description: Model chance events with sample spaces and tree diagrams, then interpret simple evidence for claims.

lessons.title: Sample Space and Theoretical Probability
objectives: List outcomes in a sample space for simple experiments
Compute probability as favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes

pedagogy.title: Start with an organized list
pedagogy.content: Write outcomes in a table or ordered list so you do not miss cases.

pedagogy.title: Equally likely assumption
pedagogy.content: Only use simple counting when outcomes are equally likely.

content.content: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. Theoretical probability is favorable outcomes over total outcomes.

content.prompt: Build a sample space table for rolling one six-sided die and flipping one coin.

exercises.question: Draw a sample space diagram for spinner outcomes {Red, Blue, Green} and coin outcomes {H, T}. Then circle outcomes where color is Blue or coin is Heads.
hints: Make a 3x2 table or a tree with six leaves.
exercises.solution: Self-check sample space: (R,H), (R,T), (B,H), (B,T), (G,H), (G,T). Favorable outcomes for Blue or Heads: 4 of 6.

exercises.question: A bag has 2 red, 3 blue, and 5 green marbles. What is P(blue)?
exercises.solution: Total marbles = 10 and blue marbles = 3, so P(blue)=3/10.

lessons.title: Probability Trees and Compound Events
objectives: Represent multi-step random experiments with a probability tree
Find probabilities of compound events by multiplying branch probabilities

pedagogy.title: One stage per branch level
pedagogy.content: Each level of the tree should represent one step of the experiment.

pedagogy.title: Why multiply branches
pedagogy.content: For independent stages, each branch narrows outcomes, so multiplying keeps only the overlap.

content.content: Tree diagrams help track compound events such as two flips or a flip followed by a die roll.

exercises.question: Draw a probability tree for: flip a fair coin, then roll a fair die. Use the tree to find P(Heads and even number).
hints: First split into H and T, then from each branch split into 1..6.
exercises.solution: Self-check: 12 equally likely outcomes, favorable are H2, H4, H6 so probability is 3/12 = 1/4.

exercises.question: A fair coin is flipped twice. What is the probability of getting exactly one head?
hints: List outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT.
Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH.
exercises.solution: 2 favorable outcomes out of 4 total, so probability is 1/2 = 0.5.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing Basics
objectives: State a simple null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis
Use sample evidence to decide whether results are unusual

pedagogy.title: Null means no change
pedagogy.content: The null hypothesis usually represents the current claim or no effect.

pedagogy.title: Not proof of truth
pedagogy.content: Failing to reject the null does not prove it is true; it only means evidence is not strong enough.

content.content: Hypothesis testing compares observed data to what we would expect under a default claim. If the observation is very unlikely, we reject the default claim.
In this course, use a simple unusualness rule: if probability under the null is less than 5%, treat the result as unusual.

exercises.question: A coin is claimed to be fair. Which is an appropriate null hypothesis?
options: The coin lands heads 50% of the time.
The coin lands heads less than 50% of the time.
exercises.solution: A fair coin means heads probability is 0.5, so that is the null hypothesis.

exercises.question: Under a fair coin model, a student gets 9 heads in 10 flips. Explain whether this seems unusual and what that suggests about the fairness claim.
hints: Estimate or look up P(9 or more heads in 10 fair flips).
exercises.solution: Self-check: P(9 or 10 heads) = 11/1024 about 1.1%, which is below 5%, so this is unusual under fairness and gives evidence against the fair-coin claim.
